clips.title: When your Theory of Change is just paperwork
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript:
Yes, this is one of the most common gaps in the sector and I have actually fixed it in practice. For example, I worked with a livelihood organization in Bihar whose TOC existed on paper but got treated as a funding document. So nobody consulted it between proposal cycles. The fix was actually not to rewrite the TOC, it was to tie each assumption in it to something the team already actually collected in their own MIS. So the the assumption that training, for example, leads to income improvement stopped sitting on a page unquestioned and became a line that the team checked against their own data every quarter.
So here's what changed on the ground, right?
Staff started naming out loud when the logic broke between an activity and its assumed outcome.
That is the actual test of whether a TOC functions as a learning tool rather than paperwork.
So if a field worker can point going to the exact step where an assumption failed last quarter.
The document is alive in that sense.
If it only gets opened for a donor visit, it's dead weight with a nice diagram.
So for small NGOs, the constraint is bandwidth, strong willingness.
Two things that actually head up in my memory in that project.
First, put the TOC review inside a meeting that already exists, like a monthly review or a quarterly board update, rather rather than inventing some kind of new ritual that nobody has the time for. And second, bring field staff into the room when the TOC gets revised, not only whoever wrote the original proposal or management. Field staff actually see where the logic fails in practice because they are the ones standing in the gap between the activity and the outcome every day. So if anyone on this AMA wants a structured way to work through this, ImpactMojo's flagship course which is free, the evidence question, monitoring evaluation. and learning for practice, covers TOC design and assumption mapping directly, and the TOC workbench lab gives you the opportunity and the place to build one out rather than just read about it.

clips.title: When five trackers won't add up
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript: Hi, this is a stage most MEL systems hit somewhere between 15 and 50 field staff. So this is a familiar bottleneck. It's not a beginner mistake. The core issue is the absence of one participant list that every program tracker refers back to. So if each of your five interventions keeps its own separate name list, you will end up with several different spellings of the same child across several. sheets. There is no way to check afterward whether your reported numbers count one child five times or five children once. Fix this before touching any dashboard. Build a master roster, I'd say with a unique ID assigned to each participant at enrollment and have every program sheet carry that ID as a column. Nothing else as identifier. That single ID is what eventually lets five separate trackers sit under one dashboard instead of existing as five unrelated files. Once the ID system exists, move data entry of shared Excel and onto a form tools such as KoBo Toolbox or Google Forms, all of which are free, feeding into sheets. Shared Excel with 40 people editing simultaneously fails in specific predictive ways. Someone overwrites a formula, someone enters a date as text instead of a date field, someone inserts a column and every downstream reference shifts one by one and nobody Nobody notices until the totals stop adding up. A form locks the structure, so a team member assigned to one program cannot enter data into another program's field by mistake. So there are programs like KoBo Toolbox for example that also supports skip logic. So each program's form only shows its questions to whoever is filling it in that day. Um, for the dashboard layer, I'd say Power BI connected live to your sheets works well at scale. There is budget for the license and the learning curve. ImpactMojo runs a course called Power BI for practitioners covering star schema design, Power Query cleaning steps and visualization using real survey data built for people without a data background. If cost is tight, a well-built pivot table structure in one master sheet pulling from the 5 program sheets by participant ID gets you most of the same value for close to no cost. Structure the dashboard, I'd say, in three layers: total reach across all five interventions at the top, program level numbers below that, indicator level only on click through. One step before building any of this is sit with each of your five program leads and get them to name the two or three indicators per intervention that would actually change a decision if the number moved. Systems built around what is easy to collect rather than what is needed to decide something terrifying. tend to collapse within a couple of quarters because nobody has the time to review 40 indicators a month. And the ones nobody reviews are the ones that stop being entered accurately. So if you want a structured way to design the indicator side, ImpactMojos MEL framework workbench lab is actually built for that step.

clips.title: Week 2: the assumptions no one revisits
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript:
Hi everyone, good morning, welcome to the week two. As you know it's Monday and we introduce our weekly challenge today, which you can work on for the next 5 days and submit it on Friday morning, so that we can review and share our inputs and learn from each other. You can share it as a form of voice note or word document. For the week one challenge, if there's anybody who wants to share their work.
It would be really helpful for us in the community to learn from each other.
The window is still open to submission.
Now let me introduce a bit background about the week two challenge.
As you must have read in the message, it's about we are talking about assumptions in theory of change.
So one part of theory of change that almost everyone writes on paper, we know there are fancy diagrams that that exist on Excel and many other frameworks. Uh, but very few people actually use, uh, one part of it that is assumptions. So assumptions are actually the conditions that need to be true for our program to work. They are the invisible if statements behind every intervention. So for example, we often assume that if people gain knowledge, they will change their behavior. But what if cultural norms, family influence, or financial constraints make that impossible? We've seen it many times.
In my experience, assumptions often look great in proposal documents.
We write them because we know they are expected.
But once implementation begins, we rarely revisit them.
Our focus is primarily on establishing that outcome indicators work.
These are the ideal indicators that can depict the change. change and hence everything that we do in evaluation design, research design is all about outcome indicators alone. And when we are asked to explain why and how the change, we often skip that part and say it's systemic, but we don't revisit the assumption that we've written. And that's where many programs struggle, not because activities were wrong, but because assumptions were never tested. So good melt. Isn't just about measuring outcomes, it's also about continuously asking, are the assumptions we started with still true? So this is a week two challenge. Uh, I happy learning to all of you. Uh, please do share, uh, examples from your own sector or your own organizations that you're working in. Uh, and happy to learn from each other.

clips.title: Breaking into the sector from political science
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript:
Hi Mohit, welcome. Political science is a genuinely useful starting point here.
Governance analysis, public systems, policy processes, a good chunk of the development sector's actual daily work sits on exactly that foundation.
So you're not starting from zero the way a purely technical graduate might be.
So let me be specific about entry paths because the social development sector covers several distant different kinds of work with different hiring logic. If you have no prior field experience, a fellowship is usually the fastest and most structured way in. Um, India fellow places you inside a grassroots organization for 13 months, uh, with a defined project and mentorship built around it. ISDM's postgraduate program in development management is more academic and cohort based, aimed at people who want a management or strategy track rather than direct field placement. Um, you also have the Gandhi Fellowship and Teach for India. Both work through education specifically. 2 years high structure, strong alumni networks if you decide to move sideways afterwards. Um, there's also the Young India Fellowship which is broader and more policy adjacent, closer to your training. Each of these takes people without prior sector experience by design, so the absence of a development studies degree is not a disqualifier for any of them. If you would rather skip the fellowship route and go straight into an organization, look at research or program associate roles at policy research bodies. PRS Legislative Research and Center for Policy Research both higher at entry level and will read your political science background as directly relevant rather than something you need to explain in interview. Electoral governance work, RTI and accountability organizations and I think think tanks doing public policy analysis are also placed. places where your degree does the talking for you. One practical thing before you send out applications anywhere is do write, write two or three short policy notes, real analysis on something you already care about, land governance, electoral reform, a state scheme, whatever pulls you. The sector hires on writing samples more than people expect, often more than the degree itself and having something concrete to send. and alongside a CV changes how quickly you get a reply. A few questions back to you since they will change what I point you towards next. Are you looking at governance and public policy specifically or are you open to on ground implementation work with a grassroots organization? And is Delhi or a particular state your base or are you open to relocating for a fellowship placement? Given where you are right now, just starting out and building the ropes, ImpactMojo is exactly the kind of of place worth joining before you commit to any one path. It puts you alongside practitioners already working across these different tracks. So you get a sense of what each one actually feels like day to day before you choose.

clips.title: A 5-step framework to test any assumption
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript: So here's a simple framework that you can use to work on testing assumptions. I'm taking an example of public health program. So first, write the assumption. It could be community health workers will conduct regular home visits. Second, what evidence would support it? Write down, it could be visit registers, beneficiary confirmations, supervisor observation. Third, Third, what evidence would challenge it? It could be missed visits, low coverage, work interview citing, workload or transport issues. Fourth, how often will you check? Monthly, for example. Fifth, what will we do if it doesn't hold? It could be you can adjust incentives, redistribute workloads or revise the implementation plan. So this is a simple framework that you can use. Uh, behind this, there's one key principle, that is, every assumption should have an evidence plan. If you can't say how you'll know whether an assumption is true, it's not yet useful for adaptive management. Thank you.

clips.title: Beyond SMART: the CREAM indicator test
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript: Hi everyone, thank you for attempting poll two of yesterday that was on indicators. And yes, the correct option is B. Um, we all know that a good indicator should do more than sound measurable. It should help you generate meaningful evidence. And you know the full form of SMART. Um, that helps you design practical indicators like. It should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time bound. What if I told you there is another framework that exists to design and assess indicator quality. It's called CREAM framework. You can read more about it in the blog that I'm attaching here. To put simply, CREAM can be expanded as clear, relevant, economic, adequate and monitorable. Means the indicator should be easy to understand and interpret. It should be closely aligned with the intended result, cost effective to measure, sufficient to capture the intended change, and data can be collected reliably over time. Just a small tip that I want to share is, if you can tell me Tell me if the indicators listed are an output or an outcome indicator. Thank you.
